sections.h2: Selling a house in East Brunswick, NJ
sections.html:
An East Brunswick owner can put the house on the market, deal directly with a cash buyer, or sell privately to someone they know. Timing decides it. A listing can draw strong interest in a township this size, but it still means staging, showings, an inspection and a lender's appraisal. A direct sale gives up some price in return for a closing date you set.

People hurry for ordinary reasons: an inheritance, a rental they are tired of managing, or a house that needs more updating than they want to fund.

  • Agent listing: works for a house in good shape when the calendar is loose.
  • Direct cash sale: works when repairs are pending, tenants are in place, or the closing date is fixed.
  • Private sale: possible if you handle the paperwork yourself, and the township's detector certificate still applies.

East Brunswick has an estimated 50,678 residents, up from 49,715 in 2020, and owners occupy eight in ten homes. The middle owned home is valued at $521,900, about $67,500 above the statewide $454,400. Growth came fast after the New Jersey Turnpike extension of 1952, when the population went from 5,699 in 1950 to 19,965 in 1960, so much of the housing is suburban stock from the decades after.

Commuting drives much of the demand. The township sits at Exit 9 of the Turnpike, and Route 18 crosses its eastern half toward New Brunswick, U.S. Route 1 and the Shore. County routes 527 and 535 pass through as well. Midtown Manhattan and Center City Philadelphia each take 45 to 60 minutes by car depending on traffic. NJ Transit's 138 goes to Port Authority in Manhattan and the 68 to Jersey City, while Suburban Transit coaches to New York leave the Transportation Center and Tower Center every 10 to 15 minutes. The typical commute is 36.5 minutes.

East Brunswick Public Schools runs 11 schools from pre-K to grade 12. Eight elementary schools cover the early grades, Hammarskjold Upper Elementary takes grades 5 and 6, Churchill Junior High takes grades 7 to 9, and East Brunswick High School takes grades 10 to 12. Confirm with the district which elementary school your street feeds before you list.

sections.h2: Do you need a Certificate of Occupancy to close?
sections.html:
No. East Brunswick neither requires nor issues a Certificate of Occupancy for residential resale or rentals. A home receives its certificate when built, and later only new improvements get inspected. Questions go to Construction Inspection at 732-390-6875.

Fire safety follows its own track. Carbon monoxide alarms near bedrooms have been mandatory in one and two family homes since April 7, 2003. In 2025 the council also adopted Ordinance 25-30, which calls for smoke and carbon monoxide detector inspections and certificates when residential units are sold, leased or newly occupied.

As introduced, the ordinance set the fee at $50 per unit with more than 10 business days of notice before the change of occupant, $75 at 4 to 10 days, and $125 under 4, plus $20 for a re-inspection after a failure. Ask the township for today's schedule and book early, since the late fee is the highest.

If the house has tenants, the ordinance reaches sales, leases and other occupancy, so time the detector inspection around the move-out or the closing date.

sections.h2: What an East Brunswick seller pays at closing
sections.html:
State law puts the realty transfer fee on the seller, and a price above $1,000,000 adds a graduated percentage charge. Your attorney or title agent can run the exact amount for your price.

  • Transfer fee: collected from the seller at filing, using a tiered rate per $500 of price.
  • Detector certificate: a township charge that climbs as the closing date nears.
  • Payoffs: your mortgage and any liens come out of the proceeds.
  • Tax form: a GIT/REP certification travels with the deed and decides whether a nonresident seller must prepay.

With no lender appraisal in a cash sale, pace depends mainly on the title search, the detector certificate and the deed filing.

The Middlesex County Clerk handles it, at the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, in New Brunswick. Weekday hours end at 4:10, but the office asks that you arrive by 4. The registry's number is 732-745-3002. The posted schedule lists $45 for a deed's first page and $10 for each page after that, with a $6 name fee in some cases. A free Property Alert service emails you whenever a filed document matches your property, a handy safeguard against surprise filings.

sections.h2: Step by step from offer to closing
sections.html:
Whether you list or sell for cash, the township side of an East Brunswick sale is short, which is part of why a quick closing is realistic here. Because no Certificate of Occupancy is required, the main local task is the detector certificate.

  1. Call Construction Inspection at 732-390-6875 and confirm what applies to your house, including any open permits from past work.
  2. Request the smoke and carbon monoxide detector inspection as soon as you have a closing date, since the fee rises as the date gets closer.
  3. Order payoff figures from your lender and ask the township for any balance owed.
  4. Have your attorney or title agent prepare the deed, the GIT/REP certification and the transfer fee.
  5. After closing, the deed is filed with the Middlesex County Clerk in New Brunswick, and the Property Alert service can tell you when it is recorded.

A buyer who pays cash can close as soon as the title work and certificate are done. A buyer who needs a mortgage adds an appraisal, a lender timeline and sometimes repair requests from the inspection.

Chapter 182 of the township code governs short-term rentals, and the council amended it through Ordinance 25-34 in 2025. If you hosted guests, read the current chapter or call the township before describing the house's rental history to a buyer.

Gather these before you accept an offer: the detector certificate request, answers from Construction Inspection on any open permits, payoff letters, and the seller's tax form for your attorney. If the house was rented to guests or tenants, add a short written history of who stayed and when, so the buyer's attorney does not have to ask for it piece by piece. Sellers who keep tidy paper trails tend to close on the date they planned.

faqs.q: Is a resale inspection mandatory in East Brunswick?
faqs.a: No Certificate of Occupancy is needed for a residential resale. A 2025 ordinance does call for smoke and carbon monoxide detector certification on sale, so ask the township how to book it.

faqs.q: What sets the timeline for a cash closing in East Brunswick?
faqs.a: The contract does. With no lender appraisal involved, the pace depends mainly on the title search, the detector certificate, and the deed filing with the Middlesex County Clerk.

faqs.q: Is the transfer fee on an East Brunswick sale mine or the buyer's?
faqs.a: It is the seller's, charged in tiers per $500 of price. Ask your attorney for the figure at your sale price.

faqs.q: Where is the deed filed after closing here?
faqs.a: With the Middlesex County Clerk, 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, New Brunswick, through the registry at 732-745-3002.

faqs.q: Can a house with tenants still be sold in East Brunswick?
faqs.a: Yes. The ordinance reaches sales, leases and other occupancy, so time the detector inspection around the tenants' move-out or the closing.
